posts.topic: New build inspections: the three windows buyers skip
posts.hook: I've seen 47 defects in a house nobody lived in.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's most arresting detail (47 defects, nobody lived there) is spent verbatim as slide 3's payoff, so the deck's biggest reveal lands as a repeat rather than a punch.
scores.fix: Keep the 47-defect line on slide 3 and rewrite slide 1 with a different withheld detail from the same story (e.g. "The worst house I ever inspected had never been slept in.") so the reveal still pays off.

posts.hook: Transplants don't leave over the heat. Month nine does it.

scores.worst_problem: The final point slide's loop, "Most buyers get this backwards," promises a reveal that the deck never delivers — it swipes into the CTA question instead of an answer, leaving one loop dangling.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 6's loop so it hands off to the closing question rather than teasing new information — e.g. "One trade-off decides it" — and sharpen slide 2's vague "Then the counting starts" into something that names what gets counted.

posts.topic: 19 months before the business paid me (delayed payoff, discipline)
posts.hook: My real estate business paid me nothing for 19 months. I almost quit in month seven.

deck.topic: 19 months before the business paid me (delayed payoff, discipline)
deck.hook: My real estate business paid me nothing for 19 months. I almost quit in month seven.

points.title: Month Seven, Broke
body: Savings gone. I took a warehouse shift four nights a week.
I told nobody in the business.
points.loop: That shift bought me something else.

points.title: The Shift Bought Time
body: With rent covered, I could say no to bad clients.
A desperate agent chases everything and closes nothing.

points.title: I Paid Myself Last
body: I picked one fixed number for my life and lived on it.
Everything above that went straight back into the business.

points.title: I Tracked Conversations
body: Ten real conversations a day. Not posts. Not likes.
Closings follow conversations. They just do not follow fast.

points.title: About Nine Months
body: The work you do today pays out roughly nine months later.
So a slow month is a report card on last spring.

points.title: Month 19
body: Three closings in one month, all from calls I made in month ten.
Nothing changed in month 19. Everything changed nine months before it.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who is nine months into something and has not seen a dollar yet.

scores.worst_problem: Two of the six loops — "The next rule was harder" and "Then month 19 happened" — are filler transitions rather than teases; the latter re-announces information the hook already gave away.
scores.fix: Rewrite the weak loops to withhold a specific new thing, e.g. replace "The next rule was harder" with "Then I cut my own pay" and "Then month 19 happened" with "Three closings, one month, zero new work."

posts.topic: Texas toll roads: the $312 first month
posts.hook: I spent $312 on tolls my first month in Dallas. I never saw a toll booth.

deck.topic: Texas toll roads: the $312 first month
deck.hook: I spent $312 on tolls my first month in Dallas. I never saw a toll booth.

points.title: No Booths, Just Cameras
body: There is nowhere to stop and pay.
A camera reads your plate at highway speed and the bill shows up weeks later.
points.loop: Not every bill finds the driver.

points.title: The Plate Pays, Not You
body: The charge goes to whoever owns the car.
Rental cars, moving trucks, a friend's SUV. Rental companies stack a daily fee on top of the toll.
points.loop: Two neighbours can pay different rates.

points.title: Tag Or No Tag
body: With a toll tag you get the lower rate.
Without one you pay the mail rate plus a fee on every invoice. Same road, same miles, bigger bill.
points.loop: The price can move by the hour.

points.title: Lanes That Reprice
body: Around Dallas and Fort Worth, some lanes cost more as traffic builds.
The sign price climbs all afternoon. The same twelve miles can triple by five.
points.loop: Your city decides most of this.

points.title: Austin, Dallas, San Antonio
body: Austin is ringed with toll roads. Dallas is stitched with them.
San Antonio has almost none. Same commute length, very different monthly cost.
points.loop: Mine added up faster than expected.

points.title: How I Hit $312
body: Thirty one days of commuting, no tag, and one week in a rental.
Mail rate on every trip, plus a fee on every invoice. A tag and one route change would have cut it close to half.
points.loop: It changed which route I drive.

cta.question: Toll road every day, or 15 extra minutes on the free route?

scores.worst_problem: The final point's loop, "It changed which route I drive," is a soft summary rather than a tease, so the swipe into the close loses tension.
scores.fix: Rewrite the last loop as a forward-pointing tease that sets up the choice, e.g. "The free route costs something too."

posts.topic: Why agents go broke after their best year (commission money habits)
posts.hook: The agents I watch quit in Texas usually had their best year right before.

deck.topic: Why agents go broke after their best year (commission money habits)
deck.hook: The agents I watch quit in Texas usually had their best year right before.

points.title: The Best Year Trap
body: A big year changes what you spend. It does not promise another big year.
So the car, the office, the lifestyle all get set at a level one good stretch paid for.

points.title: Commission Is Not Salary
body: One closing check is usually three months of work landing on a single day.
Spend it like a paycheck and you just spent a quarter of the year in three weeks.
points.loop: And one bill is already waiting.

points.title: Nobody Withholds Your Taxes
body: No employer takes anything out first. The whole check hits your account and none of it is fully yours.
I move a third into a separate account the day it lands.
points.loop: The timing is what actually hurts.

points.title: Your Work Pays 90 Days Late
body: The calls I make this week close in the spring. A quiet week today costs me nothing today.
It costs me a quarter from now, when I have forgotten why.
points.loop: Your bills run on a different clock.

points.title: Run On Your Worst Month
body: I set my fixed costs against my slowest month, not my average one.
Everything above that line is optional money, and it gets a job before it gets spent.
points.loop: You find out in year three.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who just had their biggest month and already upgraded the car.

scores.worst_problem: The hook's word order creates a garden-path stumble ('The agents I watch quit in Texas') and never names what kind of agents, forcing a reread on the one slide that can't afford one.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1 as a clean subject-first sentence, e.g. 'Most real estate agents who quit in Texas had their best year right before they walked away.', and replace the restating loop 'The spending outlives the year' with a forward tease like 'Then the checks stop matching.'

posts.topic: Price cut vs seller credit in the current Texas market
posts.hook: Texas sellers are cutting prices right now. Asking for the price cut is usually the wrong move.

deck.topic: Price cut vs seller credit in the current Texas market
deck.hook: Texas sellers are cutting prices right now. Asking for the price cut is usually the wrong move.

points.title: Homes Are Sitting
body: Across most Texas metros, houses are taking longer to sell than they did last spring.
Sellers who priced like it was 2022 are watching their listing get older every week.

points.title: The Price Cut Trap
body: Buyers ask for money off the price because it sounds like the biggest win.
Spread across 30 years, a small price cut barely moves what you pay every month.

points.title: Same 9,000 Dollars
body: Knock 9,000 off the price and your monthly change is pocket change.
Ask for that same 9,000 toward your rate instead and the monthly drop is far bigger.

points.title: Sellers Prefer This
body: A price cut lowers the number every neighbor and every future appraiser sees.
A credit at closing keeps their sale price on paper, so they agree faster.
points.loop: But there is a ceiling here.

points.title: Know The Cap
body: Your loan type limits how much a seller is allowed to hand you.
Ask above that limit and the extra money just disappears at the table.

cta.payoff: the full payment breakdown showing what a price cut and a rate credit each do to your monthly number

scores.worst_problem: The loop on slide 1 ("That changes their answer.") is ambiguous — no question has been posed, so "their answer" points at nothing, and the final loop ("Most buyers guess this wrong.") reuses the same construction as slide 3's loop, blunting both.
scores.fix: Rewrite slide 1's loop to name the stake concretely (e.g. "So ask for this instead") and vary the closing loop so it doesn't echo "Most buyers never run both."

posts.topic: Builder contracts strip five buyer protections
posts.hook: Signing a builder's contract in Texas quietly removes five protections you think you already have.

deck.topic: Builder contracts strip five buyer protections
deck.hook: Signing a builder's contract in Texas quietly removes five protections you think you already have.

points.title: Your Option Period Shrinks
body: The standard Texas contract buys you days to inspect and walk away for a small fee.
Builder contracts often give you a short review window and no exit at all.

points.title: Earnest Money Gets Big
body: Resale deals usually run about 1 percent down at signing.
Builders often want 5 percent or more, and it goes nonrefundable much sooner.

points.title: No Appraisal Protection
body: If the house appraises under your contract price, you cover that gap in cash.
Walk away instead and the builder usually keeps what you put down.
points.loop: Your closing date isn't yours either.

points.title: Closing Date Is Theirs
body: Most builder contracts let them push the finish date back, sometimes by months.
Your rate lock expires and your lease ends. Neither of those is their problem.

points.title: The Clause In The Back
body: Nearly every builder contract sends disputes to arbitration instead of a courtroom.
Their own warranty replaces what you'd normally get, and most of it runs out fast.
points.loop: One kind of home flips this.

cta.payoff: the current new builds list with the already-finished homes flagged

scores.worst_problem: The map slide immediately names all five items the hook withheld, deflating the curiosity gap the hook just opened and leaving only 'the buried fifth clause' as real pull.
scores.fix: Rewrite the map so at least three entries are consequence-framed teases rather than plain labels (e.g. 'The 5% you can't get back'), so the reader still has to swipe to learn what each protection actually is.

posts.topic: The Austin to San Antonio I-35 drive nobody warns transplants about
posts.hook: Austin to San Antonio is 80 miles. Locals still block out three hours each way.

deck.topic: The Austin to San Antonio I-35 drive nobody warns transplants about
deck.hook: Austin to San Antonio is 80 miles. Locals still block out three hours each way.

points.title: The 80 Mile Lie
body: I-35 between the two cities has been under construction for years.
The map says 80 minutes. On a bad afternoon it is three hours each way, and there is no way around it once you are in it.

points.title: Direction Decides Your Day
body: Living in San Antonio and working in Austin is a completely different drive than doing it the other way.
The heavy morning wave runs north. Drive south instead and you can save half an hour on the same road.

points.title: The 3PM Problem
body: Most Texas schools let out right around 3pm.
School traffic and the early highway wave land at the same time. Parents who planned to leave at 4 learn to leave at 2:15.

points.title: The Friday Getaway
body: On Friday afternoon, both cities empty out toward the coast and the Hill Country at once.
Leave at 4 on a Friday and you are in line with everyone else who had the same idea.

points.title: How Locals Beat It
body: People who do this drive often leave before 2 or after 7. Nothing in between.
They also pay for the toll loop east of Austin and never complain about it.

cta.question: If you had to commute it: Austin side or San Antonio side?

scores.worst_problem: The last point slide's loop, "Where you buy settles this," promises a payoff the deck never delivers — the next slide is the CTA, so the reader is teased into a dead end.
scores.fix: Replace the final loop with a line that hands off to the question instead of promising more content, e.g. "So which side wins?", and fix the hook/slide-1 mismatch by making both say miles or both say minutes.

posts.topic: The nine boring years: holding one rental beat trading four
posts.hook: The people who built real money in Texas real estate spent nine years doing nothing.

deck.topic: The nine boring years: holding one rental beat trading four
deck.hook: The people who built real money in Texas real estate spent nine years doing nothing.

points.title: Nine Years, One House
body: A client bought one rental in 2013 and never bought another.
Nine years later she still owned it.

points.title: Every Year Had An Exit
body: 2015 was a job offer in another state. 2018 was a headline saying the top was in.
2020 was a neighbor offering cash on the spot.

points.title: The Year It Cost Money
body: Roof and AC went out the same summer.
She wrote a check that wiped out two years of profit. She kept the house anyway.

points.title: The Friends Who Traded
body: Two people I know bought and sold four times in that same stretch.
Every sale meant fees, taxes, and starting a new loan over.
points.loop: The fees were the small part.

points.title: What Actually Compounds
body: Her loan got smaller every month while the rent went up.
Nobody feels that happening. It only shows up at the end.

points.title: How She Sat Still
body: She kept six months of repair money in cash and stopped checking the value online.
Boredom is a lot cheaper than panic.

cta.shareLine: Send this to someone who has been waiting for a better time to buy since 2019.

scores.worst_problem: A couple of slide loops lean on unspecified pronouns — "One of those almost worked" and "That check bought her something" — forcing a half-second of decoding about what 'worked' or what was 'bought'.
scores.fix: Name the referent in the vague loops, e.g. "The 2020 cash offer nearly won" and "That check bought nine years of rent", so the tease points at a concrete missing fact rather than an unnamed one.
